snip.t: \nLouse-borne relapsing fever\nThe human body louse, Pediculus humanus, causes itching.
3 blood-sucking human types: Body louse (Pediculus humanus corporis), Head louse (P. humanus capitis), Pubic/crab louse (Pthirus pubis)
Body louse vectors: Epidemic typhus (Rickettsia prowazekii), Relapsing fever (Borrelia recurrentis), Trench fever (Bartonella quintana) — all transcutaneous
Louse eggs (nits) found in clothing most likely belong to:

qs.q: If lice eggs (nits) are found in clothing, they are most likely from the body louse, Pediculus humanus humanus, which infests clothing and bedding, unlike head lice or pubic lice which primarily infest the hair.
qs.e: Body lice (Pediculus humanus humanus) live in clothing and bedding and lay their eggs (nits) on fabric fibers. Head lice and pubic lice primarily lay eggs attached to hair shafts.

ai.subject: Microbiology & immunology
ai.summary: Lice are blood‑sucking arthropods that infest humans, transmitting serious infections when hygiene is poor. Recognizing their life cycle and associated diseases guides prompt treatment and prevention.

sections.p: Lice are tiny, wingless insects that feed on human blood. Three species infest humans: body, head, and pubic lice, each preferring a specific niche but all capable of transmitting pathogens when conditions allow.
b: Live in hair, clothing, or pubic area

sections.p: Body lice live in clothing seams and only leave the host to feed. Head lice cling to hair shafts, while pubic lice inhabit coarse hair. All lay eggs (nits) that attach firmly to hair or fabric.
b: Eggs glued to hair or fabric

sections.p: Transmission occurs when a louse moves from contaminated clothing or bedding to a new host. The life cycle—egg, nymph, adult—takes 2–3 weeks, allowing rapid spread in crowded settings.
b: Transmission via direct contact or fomites

t.b: Dry skin reduces attachment; moist skin increases it.

sections.p: Body lice are vectors of epidemic typhus, trench fever, and relapsing fever. Head and pubic lice can cause intense itching, secondary bacterial infection, and in rare cases, bacillary angiomatosis in immunocompromised patients.
Clinical identification of lice and nits is usually sufficient. Laboratory confirmation of transmitted pathogens is done via serology or PCR when available.
b: Visual inspection of hair or clothing

t.b: Detection of bacterial DNA in blood or tissue.

sections.p: Treat the underlying infection with appropriate antibiotics; eradicate lice with topical pediculicides or mechanical removal. In low‑resource settings, washing clothing in hot water and drying on a flame is effective.

t.b: Washing at ≥50 °C removes lice and eggs.

sections.p: Remember that body lice are the only human louse that transmits serious systemic infections. In outbreak settings, focus on hygiene and clothing management.
b: Body lice = vector for typhus, trench fever, relapsing fever

whenToSeekHelp: Severe fever with rash after exposure to crowded conditions
Rapidly worsening skin infection after louse infestation
Signs of systemic infection (e.g., confusion, hypotension)

faq.a: Yes, body lice can transmit epidemic typhus, trench fever, and relapsing fever.

faq.q: How do I tell head lice from pubic lice?
faq.a: Head lice live in scalp hair; pubic lice live in coarse pubic hair and are smaller.

faq.q: What is the best way to kill lice in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: Wash clothing and bedding in hot water (≥50 °C) and dry on a flame.
